To the above we will add a letter (a most singular composition, under all the circumstances: from the only uncapturcd survivor of the Cabul Airny.Di. 1>i y don, addressed to bis brothei, and datea Jellalabad. Jan. 20 þÿ My dear Tom, þÿ Here 1 am at this place; ail safe, but not all sound, having received three wounds on the head, ieli hand, and knee, 1 have lost everything 1 had in the world . but my life has been saved in a most wonderful manner, and J am the only Euiopean who has escaped from the Cabul Army (although we have heard of two having been taken by the enemy, it is very doubilul if they will be spared ) Two natives only have reached this place, making, with myself, three persons out of an a i my ol 13,000. 1 got on very well till within about 50 miles of this, with the exception of losing all my baggage, Arc. 1 then lost the horse on which 1 was riding, Hav ing taken one of my servants, who was wounded, up behind me, we fell lather loo far in the rear, when he was pulled off from behind, and 1 fell with him. 1 was instantly felled to the earth wiih the blow of a laige knife, which wounded me in the head. 1,

however, managed to avert the second blow, by receiving my þÿenemy hand s on die edge ot my sword, by which Ins hand was somewhat damaged, and he dropped Ins kune, and made off as last as he could, and 1, following his good example, managed lo reach the mam bouy, minus inv horse. <-ap, and shoe, which last 1 lost in the snow. 1 was then trudging along, holding fast by tne tail of another officer's horse, when a native who was riding close by, said he could ride no further and told me to take his horse which I did without delay. 1 do not know who the man was, as it was quite dark at the time, but the saddle must have belonged to an Allghan. 1 now got to the front, where 1 found a number of officers, who determined to push on, as the men would obey no ordeis, and were halting every minute. We travelled on slowly all night, fired at occasionally from the sides of the hills, and found ourselves at day break about 30 miles from this, our party consisting of only seven officers, five European soldiers, holding the cantonments Gen. þÿElphinstone s and myself, the rest having lost us in the dark, and gone by some other load. At about 10 a. m. we were attacked and surrounded on all sides by horsemen ; three officers and the five Europeans were here killed One of the officers was Cicut. Bird, of the Madras Army, who fell close by my side. I with the remaining four got clear of ihe horsemen, and pushed on ; three of our party being well mounted, left the fourth and myself far in the

rear, when he, after coming on some way, said his horse was done up, and lhat lie would hide until nght, lor which purpose he left me about four miles from this He was taken and killed. I proceeded slowlv for a short time, when J saw a great many people running towards me in all directions I waited until they got pratiy close, and then pushed my horse in a gallop and ran the gauntlet for about two miles under a shower of large stories, sticks, and a tew shots, in

avaa, which i had my sword broken bv a stone, my horse shot in the spine close lo the tail, and mv hod v bruised all over by the stones. I was now attacked by a horseman, who left a party of about six, whom 1 saw leading away one of our officer's horses who had gone on ahead ; these three were killed ; and having nothing to defend myself with, and my horse being quite done up, be wounded me on the knee and hand, when, seeing me stoop down, he galloped away as last as he could, thinking, 1 suppose, that I was looking for a pistol, 1 now proceeded unmolested, and arrived here about one o'clock, quite done up, as was also rnv poor horse, who lost the use ot his hind legs next day, and died two days after without ever getting up after his arrival. If you receive this, lef them know at hotne that I am alive, as J have not been able to write since Oct. Ia«t, and perhaps we shall not have the road open when the next overland starts Since arriving here 1 have had three shirts, three pair of socks, a jacket, and a pair of trowsers giv#n to me. A verj fine stock, you will say; however, it must do until lean get another outfit. Write to me and let me know the news from home. Your affiectionate brother, þÿ William þÿBrvdon. þÿ F. S. þÿ 1 arrived here about noon ou the 13ih All further particulars you will find in the papers ; so 1 can write no more at present, it being uwkward holding my paper whilst writing."

FRANCE. The Paris papers of the 27th March are for the most part occupied with the opinions of the bureaus of the Chamber on the sugar question. The minister of commerce, in reply to the suggestion, that the manufacture of beet-toot sugar should be suppressed, declared that the chamber would not consent to any such measure until the amount of beet sugar manufactured during the last year had been ascertained, which could not be done before next session. By the French journals of the 28th, we find that the French government is really in earnest in regard to its promised disarmament. The Toulonnois of the 2ith states that a despatch bad been received at that port from the minister of marine, directing the dismissal of >1! the seamen of the fleet who had served fit? months on board a ship of war; þÿ a þÿdecision, says the Toulon nais, þÿ which is considered to be the prelude to the disarmament ol a considerable portion of our naval þÿforces. A return of the commercial navy of Fiance (taken from official documents) has been published, from which it appears that the total number of merchant vessels afloat is 15,817 ; of this number 133 are steamers.

PORTUGAL. We have accounts from Lisbon to the 21st of March. The principal event announced is the intelligence of the birth of a prince; the queen was doing well. No change of political importance had taken place, nor any other event of note beyond the arrival in the Tagus of two French ships of war, the Jena, of 84. and the Africaine, of 00 guns, for the purpose, it is said, of offering the queen a shelter under the French flag, should circumstances render such a movement necessary.

SPAIN. The marriage of the queen was beginning to be talked of in the Madrid circles. The English party, and at its head M. Mendizahnl, openly declared against the pretensions of the Bourbon family. Another party would wil- It dv accept a prince recommended by Austin but the majority seemed to incline in fa. our of one of the sons of the Infant Don Francisco de Paula. It was rumoured in Madrid that M. Gonzales entertained the strange project of marrying the Queen to the Emperor of Brazil, with a view to unite Portugal and Spain under the same crown. Queen Donna Maria would obtain in exchange the empire of Brazil, and Spain would, moreover, make over to her majesty all her former American colonies. The Madrid papers of the 22nd of March complain highly of the government for being so reserved on the supposed mealy of commerce with England, the existence of which, thev sav. was made known to the Spanish nation through the month of a foreign minister. Sir Robert Peel ; and they maintai that the report of this treaty being on foot has filled the public mind with serious apprehensions.

In Parliament the public business goes on steadily, notwithstanding the efforts of the opposition ; the premier is daily complimented with addiesses from public bodies connected with the mercantile interests in the large seaports, and the great measures of the government become every hour more and more assured of success. The corn importation bill was agreed to in the House of Peers by a majority of mote than one hundred on each great division, and in the House ofGommons there have been decisive majorities in favour of the income tax bill. Some liberals of tfie most prononci description, but w ithal men of common sense, and accustomed to practical business, declared that they felt compelled to voteagainst their party, and with the government on this measure, from a firm conviction that it was at once " hold, honest, and comprehensive." The spirit of the opposition has therefore almost wholly evaporated, and the tariff of Sir Hubert Peel will shortly lie a part ol the commercial code of the country. The income lax hill contains Its'J clauses, 88 of which were disposed of in committee on one evening.

3fi!K It has been proved impossible to get up any demonstration out of doors against this bill The people very propeilv look upon it as a part of the whole scheme; they lightly judge that if tbev have no income tax they can have no tariff; and that the tariff will tie of much more advantage to persons of small incomes than the income tax will fie injury. Provisions will fall in price at least 10 per cent þÿ manufactured articles obtained from foreign countries are to pay less duty than heretofore þÿ competition will somewhat lower the price of British manufactured goods; so that the whole result of the measure will he to tax small incomes sevenpence in the pound, and to give back at least eighteen pence. The more we consider the nature ol the measures of tier majesty's ministers, the more we are convinced that the effect will be to increase the employment of our artisans þÿ to encourage trade arid manufactures generally lo levy the burdens of the state more equably þÿ and. above all, to lead to a larger and more beneficial legislation. The facility with which money isobtainable tends lo inspire importers of goods wilti con" fidence, and cause them to reitam from pressing a large quantity tor sale ; the prices have consequently been sustained lor most articles and there is a better feeling amongst the trade generally.

We mentioned on Friday that the British Consul, Mr. Thompson, the surviving authority, and many of the inhabitants of Cape Hayti, were living in (tuts and tents, in the Ssplanade, in a truly pitiable condition. We also stated that the number of lives lost was ascertained to be six thousand, and the estimated loss of property by the foreign merchants alone two millions of dollars The scene at tms illfated place is also, we stated, described as one of complete devastation þÿ the ruins of the tiouses not exhibiting a mass of wails merely thrown down, but shewing that the. repeated upheavings of the earth had reduced the whole to a mass of rubbish, with portions of furniture protruding here and there. It might be conceived, without any stretch of imagination, that the surviving inhabitants arc subject to much want and suffering and the first feeling which rises in our minds is to send 'hem succour and relief in their destitution and distress, If any doub1 existed, however, of the necessity for a step of the kind, it will be removed when the following extract of a letter to a gentleman of this city is icad : þÿ ' 1 avail myself of the British Corvette from your place to inform you, that, through Lhvine providence, we have escaped with our lives from the dreadful effects ot the Earthquake of the 7th instant. I address you front the hospital, where the wounded ate now lying. Mv daughter O has been dangerously wounded, 1 apprehended that her leg would have to be amputated, but the timely aid rendered

by the Surgeons from Fort au-Prince lias tendered thai unnecessary, and she is improving. For myself, 1 ren amed three days under the ruins of inv house. M v daughter K. 1 thought baa perished, but a glimmering hope has reached me, which cheers my heart. 1 learn that she is on board a vessel which sailed since for Port Plata. I need not depict to you my misfortunes ; indeed ! have not the oourage to uetatl them. 1 am reduced to the lowest ebb of distress, and with only tfie suit now on mv body. In one word, my self and family sie naked, without a home, and without the means of procuring one day's subsistence. In our distress we appeal to you, and to all benevolent friends, and to the friends of humanity in your island, to aid the miserable unfortunates of thi place." And shall this appeal be made in vain ? No! 1 he inhabitants of Kingston have never yet closed their ears to the cries of the suffering, nor refused their aid to such as were in want Oh tins occasion they will prove that liiey Commisserate the Condition of the sufferers in Cape Hayu, and are ready to administer to their relief Let a subscription be immediately set on foot for the purpose, and the truth of these temarks will be exemplified. The Cape had been entirely abandoned by all who were in a condition to remove themselves, or be removed away, the aged and the wounded alone remained, it appears that on

A letter, under date 10th May, announces that Colonel Cadet, Commaiitiante of the district, had forwarded an t x press to Saint Vague to learn what was the fate of tkat town. The express, on his return, announced to the Colonel aid the inhabitants the sad intelligence that the town of Saint Vague de los Cavailleros þÿ the beautiful town of Saint Vague, which offered to the Republic of Haiti so many tesoutces in the importance of its position, and its great tiade in tobacco, had been laid tit luius Ail its edifices, its houses, had fallen, and fiad buried beneath them an incalculable number of victims of every age. Another letter of tfie 12:h May, from Porte- Plate, to another paity, cot fiuiii the first, with more fiighiful details announcing the impossibility which was found of making anv estimate of the enormous loss w hicli had taken place in a few seconds from this terrible catastrophe ! The traders ''vpriani Matin!, Domirgo Rodriguez, great Speculators in toline.ro, with

Santo Domingo þÿ The intelligence indi rectiv from Santa Domingo is siili unceitain. þÿ However, paitiesat Azua slate lhat a merchant of Azua had arrived fiom Sto Domingo, in great haste, having been there during the shock of the earthquake. The merchant is reported to have said, that of tfie thirteen large churches of Santo Domingo, one alone remain standing, named " l.a Regina " Half the houses in the town have fallen; and the others been so badly Heated, that although they had not fallen, they were yet uninhabitable. 1 here had, however, been no loss of life to deplore during the short time he remained It appears lhat all the south þÿ Miragoone, St Michel, Acqiiiu, Les Cayes, and Jeremie, have very slightly felt the shock At Anse a Veau strong fears have beeu occasioned, bv the encroachments of the sea, which Uneaten ed to overwhelm the town. Port de Paix. þÿ At Port de Paix during the shock, and while the earth was lift/ d op in the movement from south to north, the inhabitants, during some seconds, observed the sea leaving empty " Le Canal de la Torture," and retiring upon the isiatid of that name, with anger and precipitation. Such, it is described to us, remarks the Commerce, but with less force and fury, as when the red sea, dividing and rolling mountains high on each side its bed. left a passage for the Israelites to pass in their precipitate flight from Egypt. The inhabitants were also teriihlv

frightened subsequently to observe the same sea returning in a short þÿtime not to resume its bed, but to cast itself with force and in an alarming manner, upon the town, then returning to its bed dragging in all thai it encountered þÿ having drowned many persons, carrying ibeir bodies back into the channel. La Fekrikre. þÿ This citadel, which cost so many of the lives of the men and women employed in its erection þÿ which has swallowed up so many thousands of beings, has fallen, and has killed in its fall the officer of the service, and many other persons The eastern and western portions have given way, and the materials fill the ravine below, which formed the moat to the extensive and elevated entrenchments. Gonaives þÿ At Gonaives Commandant Denis, having placed himself at the head of soma of the National Guard, established older in that unfortunate place, where disorder and pillage tiad occasioned so much loss to thn unfortunate traders. þÿ Gonaives, the only town which for the last 20 years has progressed in so perceptible a manner, physically speaking, lias been just thrown back, by this deplorabla catastrophe, according to the various reports, more than 20 years, from the manner that affairs and commerce are managed in our country. All the public edifices are overthrown þÿ thirty-eight houses particularly have been, some crushed, others more or less damaged. One half ot the town is now but rubbish. The fire, occasioned during the shock, bv some vessels or demijohns containing inflamable liquid, having broken, caused the apothecary's shop of Mr Invernyzio to take fire, which occasioned the burningof lOhouses, The prison, the walls of which have beeu just re-built, has been ovei thrown, and the

prisoners to th» number of 60 or more, have made the best of the occurrence and escaped, with the exception of two, who it is said have remained In many places flames were seen to issue from the fissures and the clefs which were made duiing the strong shocks that destroyed so many tow ns In the space of 48 hours 42 shocks were counted, and the earth remained moving ss if it were flying from under the feet, with oscillations more or less marked, more or less steady as it the earth on which parties walked were suspended or rested on a mass of water. The mountain near the residence of Genera! Bonnet opened, and a large passage now remains between the two sections. The hill called " Aloine Quatre Escaliers," was so shaken, lhat a part from above became detached, and feli with much noise.

The following observations from the " Fouilie de Commerce," may interest some of our þÿreaders They refer to the Cape; " This unfortunate, dreadful, and terrific event, happened on the 7th of May, at 4 o'clock in the afternoon, and occurred with the lirst shock, þÿsuddenly and that shock was si terrible lhat all the public edifices were overthrown, broken in an instant, so much so, ihrtt it might have been said that the town was but composed of houses of card which the hand had thus overthrown, without scarce touching. But that hand is the hand of the Divinity, by means of which the Allpowerful makes himself visible þÿ makes himself felt in all that it pleases hurt to doþÿ as if to manifest to those unhappy beings who doubt there is an all powerful God þÿ thai he it is, and he alone all powerful. He has also wished to make it evident this once again how fragile is the human species, with all things which have hecn created, and thnt unknown to us, at times, the earth on which we need, aud of which we term ourselves lords, lias within its bowels the seeds, the fits t

ST! elements. of our own þÿdestruction that, in the twinkling of an eye swifter tlian speech, as swift as thought, he is ahle, this all powerful, to develope those elements, to confound þÿ swifter yet than the thoughts of the most lively imagination both our insenate pride, our irreltgion, our ingratitude to him and to our fellow mortals. These first elements, hidden within the bowels of the earth, our foster mother, according to the will of the supreme Being, iriglu be made to minister to the dissolution ot the world and of the universe, in the shortest space of time þÿ in less than a second þÿ in shorter time than it pleased him in which to create the light " Let light be, and light was " He has but to think, and not express. " Let all be nothingness," and all becomes, a thousand limes swifter than the lightening, something more horrible than chaos. Vain man! like ourselves do you þÿ then boast of your power upon this earth, our common þÿtomb which encloses, envelopes, unknown to þÿyou you who have hid nothing there þÿ under vour own feet so many elements different from yours, elements of our annihilation, as tho' we never had a being. This terrible monition added to thousands of others equally fearful and most terrific still, will it not suffice to abate that pride insensate, more than rash, which renders mankind so unhappv, during the short period left it to b eathe with difficulty and count its mishaps, draging out a languid existence, while it remains on this frail covering to its tomb, a period

ho rt indeed compared with that on which once interred, inanimate, and become dust, we shall enter. " We are informed that people from the hills and plains about the city, come with beasts bearing sacks to pillage and carry awav what may be found amid the ruins. They come, false unnatural brothers that they are, armed ftom head to foot, to rob to plunder, by violence and with armed hand, the unfortunate peoplh wounded and mutiiated by this terrible catastrophe ! What courage, just Heaven ! " Since the 8th they have commenced their terrible design The drums have been beat, hut not a soldier has presented himself. On the 9th again, but 10 alone appeared. One cannot too much commend the speed of General Motlscardi, Commandante of the district of Grande Riviere, who dispatched a detachment of the 26lh and 3rd regiments, to aid in establishing order and arresting, as much as possible, disorganization, robbery, and pillage. It is said that an example was sought to be made by way of teiror to the wretches, but a cartridge of powder was not to be procured. Il this be true, how much have the unhappy inhabitants to deplore þÿ escaped from the disaster but threatened to become a second time victims, iri tailing beneath the blows of these infamous assassins þÿ because, still living, they will not permit themselves to be quietly plundered. Victims ol the disorganization which has reigned in nature, they would become the victims of the disorder of their fellow þÿcitizens of their brothers. One may judge by this last cir-

cumstance to what point of degradation and immorality this young nation has fallen þÿ if the facts be true. Hamburg, Ma 14 þÿ Evcrv day brings us fresh proofs of the sympathy which the heavy calamity that has befallen this city occasions throughout Germany. By the Hamburg Correspondenten of this date it appears that the number of houses destroyed (exclusive ol public buildings and warehouses) is now ascertained to be 1740, and the worth of these dwelling houses alone is estimated at 47.0(10, 000 of marks current, or about 2.000 000 1.

MEETING AT THE MANSION-HOUSE ON FRIDAY. A meeting of the merchants, bankers, and traders of the city of London, was held at the Mansion-house yesterday, tor the purpose of increasing the fund which has already been so promptly raised for alleviating the sufferings of the citizens of Hamburg who have been rendered houseless by the recent destructive and disastrous fire in that city. The Lord Mayor took the chair shortly alter one o'clock, and said that he had no doubt that his fellow citizens would respond to the call which was about to be made on them, with that liberality with which thev were always known to come forward when any teal cause of distress railed for their assistance. (Hear, and cheers). Air r. Baring proposed the first resolution, and said theie never was a case which made a stronger appeal to the generosity of the British public, and dwelt upon the facts which had been staled by Mr. Colqnhoun in tire document which he had reao to t lie meeting. This was a case in which their aid would be of immediate efficacy. Hamburg was at our very doors, and the subscriptions raised to day might feed the starving population of that city by Tuesday next. (Hear) Let it not be said that because we had poor of our own we were not to assist and relieve the sufferings of our foreign brethren. He concluded bv moving the resolution expressive of sympathy with the sufferers by the distressing calamity, r\lr. W. Altwood seconded the lesolutiom which was put by the Lord Mayor, and

adopted unanimously. Sir J Itae Keid moved the next resolution. He thought he should best discharge his duty by not encroaching on their time, but by sir rtly reading an extract from a letter he bad received bom Hamburg but one hour before ibr meeting look place ; it was dated Mav 17, ami staled that throughout the city the inhabi- tants " seemed overwhelmed with the kind, the more than kind, the truly noble expression of sympathy on the part of the merchants and bankers of London. Every exertion that can be made will be made, but it is impossible that any words ot mine can describe the misery and distress thai now prevail. They are beyond description. He moved the fourth resolution : þÿ " That the thanks of this meeting arc also due. and are hereby given to her Majesty's government, for the supply of tents arid blankets from the public stores, spontaneously afforded for the use of the homeless population of Hamburg.'' ft was then proposed that subscriptionbooks lie opened at the London and country bankers. I hanks were voted to the Lord Mayor for the use ot the hall, and for his lordship presiding at the meeting ; after which the meeting separated.

The subscriptions in aid of the Hamburg sufferers are making the most successful progress both here and on the Continent. Lloyd's subscriptions closed on Thursday, and amounted to 355/ 10s. The King of I'russia has forwarded 5000 golden fredericks and 3000 blankets. The King of Denmark has given 400.000 marks, and J'rinee Mecklenburg Srbwerin 30,000 marks. In Bremen 20.000 thalers were subscribed, arid 150 waggon-loads of bread. At Aix la Chapelle,

Liege, Cologne, Ghent, Dusscluoif, and Wisbrden, a series of musical fetes have been organized for the benefit of the sufferers, in addition to various donations by the chief rt sidents both in mbney, dollies, and blankets. The most lively sympathy appeals to prevail in behalf of all who have lost property by this coriffagiation ; and so sensible aic the sufferers themselves of the extent of it, that several private letters received Iroui Dumbing state, on hchall of these, their sorrow and regret at the Lnglish having in any oik instance been personally annoyed either by word or deed in the contusion which lollowed the liist alaitn. To the English, as well as all other people who have subscribed to mitigate then uigent necessities, thev uestre to be represented as exceedingly grateful for the aid so seasonably extended to them, and speak with pride of r lie generous sympathy excited in their behalf at a per.od when commercial distress generally prevailed.

Violent Shocks of Earthquake. þÿ Letters from Athens of the 2Sih ult. stale, that several violent shocks of an earthquake we>e felt in vai ious parts of the Peloponnesus ; on the 18th, at Sparta, the shocks lasted from 25 to 30 seconds each. 1 he inhabitants ran terrified out ol their houses. On tfie same day, and in the course of the night, four or five other slighter shocks wrote experienced. Beyond the Eurotas an immense rock fell from Mount Menelas, near the village of Drouchas. An old tower situate in the town of Magoules was thrown to the ground. At Mistra the soil trembled with more violence than at Sparta, and a portion of the Hellenic College and several houses were destroyed. The water of the springs and wells became turbid, and an enormous roek, having detach ed itself from the summit of old Mount Mistra, rolled with terrific noise into the lowri. At Ca lames the first shock, felt at half past nine o'clock, lasted between 40 and 50 seconds, and there were ten others, from thai hour until midnight, at intervals of three quaners of an hour. Most of the houses were damaged, and several in the neighbourhood actually gave way. Upwaids of 50 dwellings were thrown down at Areepolis, and 15 low ers crumbled at GStvius Many pel sous were buried under ihe ruins of their houses in the province of Mama.

Upon the arrival of the news in London, nothing could exceed the deep feeling of regret which were exhibited by the members of the commercial world, for hundreds of persons residing in England are great sufierers by this most deplorable calamity. One body particularly are sufierers to an enormous extent, þÿ we allude to the London fire offices, which, from the spirit that has hitherto characterised their business, have effected insurances to an immense amount throughout all most every country in Europe, more especially in the Hanseatic towns from their immediate connexion with England. The gross loss to these companies is supposed to amount to nearly 1,000,000/. sterling. TERMINATION OP THE PIKE AND EXTENT OP THE DESTRUCTION. Hamburg, Monday Morning, May, 9 The fire has ceased, and we are at length reassured against its breaking out afresh from the smouldering ruins, as it was feared last night would be again the ease. What with the cessation of successive gale of wind from different points of the compass, the occurrence ol abundant rain, the blowing up, batiering, and pulling down of houses, with the continuous workings of a great number of engines on two points to which the fir had been confined by the encountering in ita progress a large sheet of water (the Alster,) tins fearful element had lost sufficient of ita magnitude and power to become within control at about ten on the morning of Sunday, alter having teen up to that lime raging for upwards of three days and nights. Three-eights of the town are now in ruina. More than 60 streets and 2.000 houses and Warehouses, being property ol seveial millions in value, have been thus annihilated in comparatively a lew short hours. The loss of life, it was throughout thought, must be great, but tiie report of casualties, and the discovery of human remains anud the ruins up to tins time, the beginning of a dealing promi-e that it will prove far greater than was conceived. 7 he fire, it is ascertained, broke out in a cigar manufactory, held by a Jew, who ic now ariested under strong suspicion ol having been its intentional author. !So great was the confidence of the people that the fire would be immediately got under, that up to the burning <-f St. Nicholas Church, few moved propeitv from their houses till about

This confidence has been their ruin ; some forty years ago they may have been probably equal, if not superior to any other city in that respect ; but now, most assuredly, are their fire engines not far from half a century bwhind ours.
